anchor.text:
Introducing: PlayerZero

The world's first Engineering World Model that puts debugging, fixing, and testing your code on autopilot.

We've raised $20M from Foundation Capital, @matei_zaharia (Databricks), @pbailis (Workday), @rauchg (Vercel), @zoink (Figma), @drewhouston (Dropbox), and more

PlayerZero frees up 30% of your engineering bandwidth by:
1.⁠ ⁠Finding the root cause for bugs & incidents in minutes that engineering teams take days to identify.
2.⁠ ⁠Predicting in minutes, edge case issues that a 300-person QA team would take weeks to find.

------

Here's why this matters:

No one in your org has a complete picture of how your production software actually behaves.

Support sees tickets. SRE sees infra. Dev sees code. Each team builds their own fragmented view - and none of these systems talk to each other. When something breaks, everyone scrambles to stitch the picture together by hand.

PlayerZero connects all of it into a single context graph -

→ The Slack thread where your lead said "we went with X because Y fell apart in prod last time"
→ The PR review where an engineer explained the tradeoff
→ The lifetime history of your CI/CD pipeline, observability stack, incidents, and support tickets

So you can trace any problem to its root cause across every silo.

And it compounds. Every incident diagnosed teaches the model something new. The longer it runs, the deeper it understands - which code paths are high-risk, which configurations are fragile, which changes tend to break which customer flows.

So when you sit down to debug a live issue, you have your entire org's collective reasoning and production memory behind you - instantly.

------

Zuora, Georgia-Pacific, and Nylas have reduced resolution time by 90% and caught 95% of breaking changes and freeing an average of $30M in engineering bandwidth.

------

Our guarantee:

If we can't increase your engineering bandwidth by at least 20% within one week, we'll donate $10,000 to an open-source project of your choice.

Book a demo - https://bit.ly/3NlLMeN

gen1.text:
It seems as if writing code is mostly solved. Keeping it alive in production after you ship it is the actual bottleneck.

A 26-year-old ex-OpenAI researcher out of Stanford just raised $20M to kill traditional QA testing.

Here is the breakdown:

* The Tech: PlayerZero’s Sim-1 model takes a code change and cross-references it against real production data to predict what will break.

* The Accuracy: 92.6% across 3,000+ real production scenarios. It's currently beating both Claude Code and Codex at accurate code simulations.

* The Impact: It does in minutes what a 300-person QA team does in weeks. For a 50-engineer team, it eliminates roughly 30,000 hours of test writing per year.

The cap table is a who's who of tech royalty: CEOs of Figma, Dropbox, Vercel, and Databricks.

Introducing: PlayerZero

The world's first Engineering World Model that puts debugging, fixing, and testing your code on autopilot.

We've raised $20M from Foundation Capital, @matei_zaharia (Databricks), @pbailis (Workday), @rauchg (Vercel), @zoink (Figma), @drewhouston (Dropbox), and more

PlayerZero frees up 30% of your engineering bandwidth by:
1.⁠ ⁠Finding the root cause for bugs & incidents in minutes that engineering teams take days to identify.
2.⁠ ⁠Predicting in minutes, edge case issues that a 300-person QA team would take weeks to find.

------

Here's why this matters:

No one in your org has a complete picture of how your production software actually behaves.

Support sees tickets. SRE sees infra. Dev sees code. Each team builds their own fragmented view - and none of these systems talk to each other. When something breaks, everyone scrambles to stitch the picture together by hand.

PlayerZero connects all of it into a single context graph -

→ The Slack thread where your lead said "we went with X because Y fell apart in prod last time"
→ The PR review where an engineer explained the tradeoff
→ The lifetime history of your CI/CD pipeline, observability stack, incidents, and support tickets

So you can trace any problem to its root cause across every silo.

And it compounds. Every incident diagnosed teaches the model something new. The longer it runs, the deeper it understands - which code paths are high-risk, which configurations are fragile, which changes tend to break which customer flows.

So when you sit down to debug a live issue, you have your entire org's collective reasoning and production memory behind you - instantly.

------

Zuora, Georgia-Pacific, and Nylas have reduced resolution time by 90% and caught 95% of breaking changes and freeing an average of $30M in engineering bandwidth.

------

Our guarantee:

If we can't increase your engineering bandwidth by at least 20% within one week, we'll donate $10,000 to an open-source project of your choice.

Book a demo - https://t.co/dH1dulIwSS

- Tools like Cursor and Claude Code made writing code 10x faster.

What used to take 300 QA engineers a week now takes a day.
We optimized writing code 
Nobody optimized surviving it.
As AI builders, this is the missing piece for truly reliable agentic systems. What’s your biggest scaling worry with AI-generated code?

vibe coding has a massive blind spot that nobody's really talking about

we're shipping code 100x faster than ever with claude code, codex, cursor, all of it

but the tooling to catch what breaks after you ship... hasn't kept up AT ALL

right now when something goes wrong, you (+ your team) have to manually dig through logs, tickets, and old slack threads to figure out what happened and why

that context is scattered across 10 different tools and nobody has the full picture

engineering teams are already spending most of their time just investigating bugs instead of building

this is especially painful for non-technical vibe coders (like me!!)

playerzero is solving this in a way i think is really smart

it absorbs your entire codebase history (every bug, outage, customer ticket, etc) into one knowledge graph

(basically a map of how everything in your software connects to everything else)

so say a payment webhook broke 2 months ago. then today someone touches similar code.

1. playerzero checks it against the graph
2. sees the connection
3. and flags it before it hits production.

if something does slip through, it triages the issue and patches it before a customer even notices

The world's first Engineering World Model that puts debugging, fixing, and testing your code on autopilot.

PlayerZero frees up 30% of your engineering bandwidth by:

------

Here's why this matters:

No one in your org has a complete picture of how your production software actually behaves.

Support sees tickets. SRE sees infra. Dev sees code. Each team builds their own fragmented view - and none of these systems talk to each other. When something breaks, everyone scrambles to stitch the picture together by hand.

PlayerZero connects all of it into a single context graph -

→ The Slack thread where your lead said "we went with X because Y fell apart in prod last time"
→ The PR review where an engineer explained the tradeoff
→ The lifetime history of your CI/CD pipeline, observability stack, incidents, and support tickets

So you can trace any problem to its root cause across every silo.

And it compounds. Every incident diagnosed teaches the model something new. The longer it runs, the deeper it understands - which code paths are high-risk, which configurations are fragile, which changes tend to break which customer flows.

So when you sit down to debug a live issue, you have your entire org's collective reasoning and production memory behind you - instantly.

------

Zuora, Georgia-Pacific, and Nylas have reduced resolution time by 90% and caught 95% of breaking changes and freeing an average of $30M in engineering bandwidth.

------

Our guarantee:

gen1.text:
Every AI team is obsessing over writing code faster.

Almost no one is asking: what happens after that code hits production?

We run agents that touch thousands of transactions a week inside Fortune 5000 finance teams and supply chains. When something breaks at 3am, it’s not a GitHub notification 
 it’s a CFO calling because month-end close just stalled.

As coding tools get better, code velocity explodes. But code quality, QA capacity, and on-call processes don’t magically scale with it.

That creates a growing gap:

More PRs, more surface area, more edge cases.

The same QA process you had when engineers wrote everything by hand.

That math doesn’t work.

PlayerZero is built for exactly that gap.

It:

Runs deep QA on every commit.

Detects, triages, and helps resolve bugs autonomously.

Acts like an always-on support engineer, so your on-call isn’t getting paged five nights in a row for the same class of issues.

The key to making this work in the enterprise isn’t just “better tests.” It’s context.

Generic testing tools don’t understand:

Your codebase and architectural patterns.

Your real-world edge cases.

Your production environment and business-critical flows.

PlayerZero learns that context over time. It builds a working model of how your system behaves and what “normal” looks like in your specific business. That’s the same principle we use when deploying agents for customers: the system has to understand your business, not just run generic checks.

2.⁠ ⁠Predicting in minutes, edge case issues that a 300-person QA team would take weeks to find.

------

Here's why this matters:

No one in your org has a complete picture of how your production software actually behaves.

Support sees tickets. SRE sees infra. Dev sees code. Each team builds their own fragmented view - and none of these systems talk to each other. When something breaks, everyone scrambles to stitch the picture together by hand.

PlayerZero connects all of it into a single context graph -

→ The Slack thread where your lead said "we went with X because Y fell apart in prod last time"
→ The PR review where an engineer explained the tradeoff
→ The lifetime history of your CI/CD pipeline, observability stack, incidents, and support tickets

So you can trace any problem to its root cause across every silo.

And it compounds. Every incident diagnosed teaches the model something new. The longer it runs, the deeper it understands - which code paths are high-risk, which configurations are fragile, which changes tend to break which customer flows.

So when you sit down to debug a live issue, you have your entire org's collective reasoning and production memory behind you - instantly.

Zuora, Georgia-Pacific, and Nylas have reduced resolution time by 90% and caught 95% of breaking changes and freeing an average of $30M in engineering bandwidth.

gen1.text:
Over the last 2 years I’ve been building with AI-assisted development, and the last ~6 months heavily with agents

One thing has become very clear:
Writing code is no longer the bottleneck. Writing reliable code is.

Most of the pain now shows up after you ship:

🔶 edge cases tests didn’t catch
🔶 bugs that only appear in production
🔶 time lost digging through logs, metrics, and tickets
🔶 incidents that feel like they shouldn’t have happened

AI made it easier to write code fast, but it didn’t solve how that code behaves in real systems

That’s the harder problem

I came across @playerzero_ai  and really like the approach. They focus on the part most tools ignore:

🔶 simulating how code behaves before it goes live
🔶 improving QA without relying on brittle test cases
🔶 helping trace and resolve production issues faster

It feels less like another dev tool and more like something that helps you actually run software in production

PlayerZero turns it into a real one:

→ permanent

The system already knows:
→ what changed
→ what depended on it
→ and why that path exists

That’s the real unlock.

Not better debugging.

But turning institutional knowledge into infrastructure.

Feels like a world model moment.

This is the real bottleneck in software teams: the code is in 1 place, but the reasoning is scattered across 10 places. If a model can actually join that back together, that is super useful.

Just launched PlayerZero is claiming to do that. 

Current coding agents are mostly good at working on code in front of them, but production failures usually come from missing context outside the code. The real story of a bug is spread across pull request comments, Slack decisions, incident timelines, logs, deployment history, support tickets, monitoring, and weird old tradeoffs nobody documented cleanly.

So they built "the world's first Engineering World Model that puts debugging, fixing, and testing your code on autopilot."

A system that tries to connect all those scattered signals into 1 reasoning layer. Then it uses that layer for 2 jobs: root cause analysis after something breaks, and bug prediction before code ships.

Their self-reported benchmark against real production tickets.
64% of PlayerZero’s flagged issues later became actual tickets, vs 16.3% for Cursor BugBot and 11% for Claude Code.

founderFollowups.text:
Context graphs will be to the 2030s what databases were to the 2000s.

Within a year, every frontier lab will be building one and here's why:

At 10 people, coordination is free. Everyone knows what everyone else is doing. You never hold a meeting to "align."

At 100 people, you spend maybe 20% of your payroll on coordination. Managers, syncs, standups, planning sessions, status reports.

At 10,000 people, that number approaches 60%. The majority of your headcount exists not to produce anything but to make sure the people who produce things are producing the right things in the right order.

This is the dirty secret of large organizations: output scales linearly with headcount, but coordination cost scales exponentially. Every person you add creates new information pathways that must be maintained. The hierarchy is the protocol that manages this, and it's brutally expensive.

Hierarchy is a compression algorithm for organizational knowledge. At every layer, a manager compresses the reality of their team into a summary that fits in a 30-minute meeting with their boss. Their boss compresses eight of those summaries into one for their boss. By the time information reaches the CEO, it's been lossy-compressed through five or six layers of human interpretation.

This is why CEOs make bad decisions.  The information they receive has been compressed, filtered, and distorted at every layer. The hierarchy is high-latency, low-bandwidth, and lossy.

Jack didn't fire 4,000 producers but cut 4,000 compression nodes. Block's "world model" is a replacement algorithm. Zero latency, high bandwidth, lossless. Every person at the edge gets the full picture without waiting for information to travel through human relays.

The infrastructure that makes this possible is the context graph. A living, continuously updated representation of how the organization actually works. Not just data, but decision traces: the reasoning connecting observations to actions. Not what's true now, but why it became true.

The shift from "give agents memory" to "give agents organizational judgment" will define the next platform war

founderFollowups.text:
Introducing: PlayerZero

The world's first Engineering World Model that puts debugging, fixing, and testing your code on autopilot.

We've raised $20M from Foundation Capital, @matei_zaharia (Databricks), @pbailis (Workday), @rauchg (Vercel), @zoink (Figma), @drewhouston (Dropbox), and more

PlayerZero frees up 30% of your engineering bandwidth by:
1.⁠ ⁠Finding the root cause for bugs & incidents in minutes that engineering teams take days to identify.
2.⁠ ⁠Predicting in minutes, edge case issues that a 300-person QA team would take weeks to find.

------

Here's why this matters:

No one in your org has a complete picture of how your production software actually behaves.

Support sees tickets. SRE sees infra. Dev sees code. Each team builds their own fragmented view - and none of these systems talk to each other. When something breaks, everyone scrambles to stitch the picture together by hand.

PlayerZero connects all of it into a single context graph -

→ The Slack thread where your lead said "we went with X because Y fell apart in prod last time"
→ The PR review where an engineer explained the tradeoff
→ The lifetime history of your CI/CD pipeline, observability stack, incidents, and support tickets

So you can trace any problem to its root cause across every silo.

And it compounds. Every incident diagnosed teaches the model something new. The longer it runs, the deeper it understands - which code paths are high-risk, which configurations are fragile, which changes tend to break which customer flows.

So when you sit down to debug a live issue, you have your entire org's collective reasoning and production memory behind you - instantly.

------

Zuora, Georgia-Pacific, and Nylas have reduced resolution time by 90% and caught 95% of breaking changes and freeing an average of $30M in engineering bandwidth.

------

Our guarantee:

If we can't increase your engineering bandwidth by at least 20% within one week, we'll donate $10,000 to an open-source project of your choice.

Book a demo - https://t.co/dH1dulIwSS
